questions.q: When is the ultimate time to pull the goalie?
questions.headline: Down one, anywhere from 2:20 to 4:40 left; down two, about 3:45. Most teams wait too long, but it costs less than you'd think.
body: With an extra skater, a team down one late scored 7.4 goals per 60 minutes but allowed 22.2 into the empty net; with the goalie in, 2.4 for and 2.3 against.

Feeding those rates into a second-by-second model, the chance of tying a one-goal game is highest (42.3%) when the goalie comes out with 2:20 to 4:40 left: a wide, flat top. NHL teams typically pulled at 1:46, which gets 41.9%. Never pulling gets 40.0%.
Down two, the best time is about 3:45 left (14.8% to tie vs 14.7% at the usual 2:34). The empty-net goals against cost little: losing by two counts the same as losing by one.

chart.title: Chance to tie a one-goal game, by when the goalie is pulled

questions.method: Third periods of 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular-season games. Goal rates for teams trailing by one (and two) measured at 5-on-5 with the goalie in and 6-on-5 with it pulled, then a second-by-second model of the race to a tying goal for every possible pull time. Assumes rates don't change with the clock; a goal against ends the chase.

questions.q: How much do faceoff wins actually matter?
questions.headline: A little. Going from 50% to 55% on faceoffs is worth about 0.8 goals a season.
body: In the 30 seconds after a 5-on-5 faceoff, the winner's goal difference is +1.8 per 100 wins in the offensive zone, +0.3 at center and -0.5 in its own zone (still deep in its end, a win only limits the damage).
Spread over a season, a team winning 55% instead of 50% gains roughly 0.8 goals (about 0.1 wins). Across team-seasons, faceoff percentage and goal share correlate at r = 0.17.
The edge is real but short-lived: after half a minute, possession has usually changed hands several times.

chart.title: Goal edge for the faceoff winner in the next 30 seconds (per 100 wins, 5-on-5)

questions.method: Every 5-on-5 faceoff in 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular seasons: goals for minus against for the winning team until the next faceoff or 30 seconds, by zone (zone from the winner's side). Season estimate assumes ~58 faceoffs a game, 62% at 5-on-5.

questions.q: Do fights change the momentum of a game?
questions.headline: Not measurably. Teams losing the shot battle before a fight recover about as much as they do without one.
body: Before a fight, the team losing the shot battle had 38.2% of attempts over the previous 10 minutes. In the 10 minutes after, it had 50.5%.

That looks like a momentum swing, but random moments with the same starting share bounce back just as much (to 49.7%), because lopsided stretches rarely last. The fight's own effect: +0.7 points (90% range -0.4 to +1.7).
So the swing fans see after a fight is mostly regression to the mean, not the fight.

chart.title: Shot-attempt share of the team that was behind, next 10 minutes

questions.method: Fighting majors in 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular seasons (5th to 50th minute). Shot attempts (goals, shots, misses, blocks) 10 minutes before and after. Expected = what random non-fight moments in the same games did from the same starting share (a linear fit), so regression to the mean is removed.

questions.q: Is a two-goal lead the worst lead in hockey?
questions.headline: No. Teams that went up two won 88% of the time, vs 68% after going up one.
body: Once a team led by one, it won 68.4% of those games. Once it led by two, 87.5%. By three, 96.6%.
The 'worst lead' line comes from how a blown two-goal lead feels: the comeback gets remembered and the many routine wins don't. Every extra goal of cushion raised the chance of winning.

chart.title: Won the game after first leading by…

questions.method: Every regular-season game in 2024-25 and 2025-26: the first time each team led by 1, 2 or 3 goals in regulation, and whether it won (including overtime and shootouts).
questions.sample: 3,552 one-goal leads, 2,204 two-goal leads, 1,278 three-goal leads

questions.q: How much does a back-to-back hurt?
questions.headline: About 7 points of win probability: tired teams won 41% against rested ones, vs 48% expected.
body: On the second night of a back-to-back against a team that had rested, teams won 40.8% of the time. From their records in rested games and home ice, we'd have expected 48.1%.
The gap is -7.3 points (90% range -10.7 to -3.8), worth about 0.15 standings points per game. Part of it is the backup goalie who usually starts those nights.

chart.title: Win rate on the second night of a back-to-back vs a rested team

questions.method: 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular seasons. A back-to-back = played the day before; the opponent had at least one day off. Expected = each team's win rate in its rested games (lightly shrunk) combined with the opponent's and league home-ice advantage (log5).

questions.q: How much does scoring first matter?
questions.headline: A lot: the team that scored first won 67% of games.
body: Scoring first, home teams won 69.6% and road teams 63.0%.
Timing matters: an opening goal in the first period led to a win 64.6% of the time; when the first goal came in the third, 90.3%.
Part of this is selection: better teams score first more often. But a one-goal head start is a real edge in a low-scoring game.

chart.title: Won the game after scoring first

questions.method: Every 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular-season game with a goal in regulation or overtime: did the team that scored first win (including overtime and shootouts)?

questions.q: How often does the team leading after two periods win?
questions.headline: 86% of the time. Up one: 76%. Up two: 91%. Up three or more: 98%.
body: Teams ahead after 40 minutes won 85.6% of games. A one-goal lead held 76.1% of the time, two goals 90.9%, three or more 98.1%.
Games tied after two went to overtime 39.2% of the time.

chart.title: Won the game when leading after two periods by…

questions.method: Score after 40 minutes in every 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular-season game and the final result (overtime and shootouts included).

questions.q: What's the most dangerous kind of shot?
questions.headline: Anything from right on top of the goalie: 13% of shots within 10 feet go in, twice the average. Next: rebound (11%).
body: Of unblocked shots, 6.6% became goals. Within 10 ft shots went in 13.3% of the time, rebound 11.1%, 10 to 20 ft 10.6%.

A rebound from under 20 feet goes in 12.8% of the time. Distance dominates everything else, which is why our expected-goals model leans on it first, then on rebounds and how the puck moved just before the shot. (The play-by-play has no passes, so one-timers and cross-ice feeds can only be inferred.)
The least dangerous: from the point (over 50 ft) (1.4%).

chart.title: Share of unblocked shots that became goals

questions.method: Unblocked, non-empty-net regulation shots in 2024-25 and 2025-26 (NHL play-by-play). Categories overlap (a rebound can also be from close in). Rebound = a shot within 3 seconds of the same team's previous shot; rush = within 4 seconds of an event in the neutral or defensive zone.

questions.q: How much of a goalie's season is luck?
questions.headline: Most of it: roughly 69–81% of the spread between goalies in one season is luck.
body: For goalies facing 1,000+ unblocked shots, the differences in goals saved above expected are what you'd see if 81% of them came from chance (which shots happened to go in), not skill.
The share is 76% for goalies with 500+ shots and 69% for workhorses with 1,500+ (a smaller, more selected group, so the estimates bounce around). Either way, luck is the bigger part.
That's why our player values shrink goalie results hard toward average, and why one great season predicts the next one only weakly (year-to-year correlation about 0.14).

chart.title: Share of the goalie spread that's luck, by shots faced

questions.method: MoneyPuck goalie seasons 2022-23 to 2025-26, all situations. Luck share = the average binomial variance of goals saved above expected per shot (from each goalie's own expected save rate and shot count) divided by the observed variance across goalies.

questions.q: When does a power play actually score?
questions.headline: Not early. The first 15 seconds are the slowest; after that the pace is steady to the end.
body: Scoring pace in the first 15 seconds of a 5-on-4: 0.20 goals per two minutes, -19% vs the power play's average (0.24). From 30 seconds on it stays within a narrow band; the busiest slice is 105–120s.
The first 30 seconds produce 25% of power-play goals while taking up 29% of power-play time. The opening faceoff has to be won and the set-up established before the chances come.
Overall, 19.3% of these power plays scored.

chart.title: Power-play scoring pace by time into a 5-on-4 (goals per 2 minutes)

questions.method: Two-minute minors that created a 5-on-4 in 2024-25 and 2025-26 regular seasons (not in the last minute). Time on the power play and power-play goals counted in 15-second slices until a goal, two minutes, or a change in strength.
